findings.title: limitFunction drops every argument passed to the returned wrapper
findings.cause: The wrapper returned by limitFunction is declared as return () => limit(() => function_()), so it never captures or forwards ...arguments_ to function_. This contradicts index.d.ts, which returns (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>.
findings.impact: Any exported limited function that depends on parameters receives no arguments. Real callers get wrong results, undefined inputs, or failed requests while TypeScript still advertises argument forwarding.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 returns a zero-argument wrapper. index.d.ts:133-136 types the returned function as accepting the original Arguments. Runtime probe output: {"result":"","calls":[[]]} after calling limited('a', 42). git diff also shows the prior implementation was return (...arguments_) => limit(() => function_(...arguments_)).

findings.title: Options object changes rejectOnClear default and accepts falsey non-booleans
findings.cause: The options destructuring uses rejectOnClear = true, while the public docs and type docs state Default: false. The validation also only checks truthy values with if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'), so values such as 0, '', and null are accepted even though rejectOnClear is documented and typed as boolean.
findings.impact: pLimit({concurrency: 1}) unexpectedly rejects queued promises on clearQueue(), unlike pLimit(1) and unlike the documented default. Invalid falsey option values silently alter behavior instead of failing early.
findings.evidence: index.js:4-13 sets rejectOnClear to true for option objects and only validates truthy non-booleans. readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document rejectOnClear as boolean with Default: false. Runtime probe for pLimit({concurrency: 1}) produced {"settled":true,"status":"rejected","name":"AbortError","message":"This operation was aborted"} for a pending task after clearQueue(). A second probe showed {"value":0,"threw":false}, {"value":"","threw":false}, and {"value":null,"threw":false}.

findings.title: limit.map passes undefined index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call now passes iterableIsArray ? index : undefined, so Set and iterator inputs do not receive the numeric index even though Array.from supplies one for all iterables.
findings.impact: The documented map contract is broken for Sets, iterator objects, and other non-array iterables. Callers using the index for output paths, batching, stable IDs, or logging receive undefined.
findings.evidence: index.js:106-113 passes undefined as the index when Array.isArray(iterable) is false. readme.md:78-85 says the mapper receives the item value and its index and is equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)). index.d.ts:40-43 types mapperFunction as (input, index: number). Runtime probe with new Set(['a','b','c']) returned ["a:undefined","b:undefined","c:undefined"].

findings.title: validateConcurrency rejects previously supported Infinity concurrency
findings.cause: The validator now requires Number.isInteger(concurrency) && concurrency > 0. The local git diff shows the previous condition also allowed concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY.
findings.impact: Callers using pLimit(Infinity) as an explicit no-limit mode now get a TypeError, even though the prior implementation accepted it. This is an edge-case compatibility regression.
findings.evidence: index.js:127-130 rejects Infinity. git diff -- index.js shows the validator changed from ((Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0) to Number.isInteger(concurrency) && concurrency > 0. Runtime probe output: {"value":"Infinity","accepted":false,"name":"TypeError","message":"Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up"}.
